<reason>Both sides were strong, but PRO built the cleaner decision rule. PRO's fork — if the low price survives being named, disclosure is costless; if naming kills it, the "discount" was revenue harvested from ignorance — absorbed CON's central ratchet mechanism and converted it into a normative point PRO was happy to own (ban as the honest remainder). CON's sharpest work was the verification-gate distinction (student ID vs. spoofable device/postcode signals), which genuinely broke PRO's published-discounts analogy, and the excellent catch that PRO's most vivid example (midnight plumber) is a condition-of-sale outside PRO's own bright line — a hit PRO never answered. But CON's welfare story never squarely met PRO's claim that algorithms sort by urgency and inability to walk away rather than ability to pay, and CON's own concession in [B4.1] that the unsophisticated already pay the most today left CON defending an "imperfect mechanism" whose low prices flow disproportionately to the sophisticated — a tension PRO exploited hard in closing. PRO also answered CON's enforceability challenge with a concrete, non-brittle swap test rather than dodging; CON's reply (can't fix "the moment," shadow shoppers get fingerprinted) was plausible but did not fully kill it. Against PRO: the Rebuttal 1 clip is an execution cost, and the "no answer" jab in [A4.5]–[A4.6] was premature given the format's answer slot. Net: PRO carried the low burden created by the motion's disjunction and "usually," and made the choice easier to resolve.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's [B2.1]–[B2.3] verification-gate response was the single most damaging strike, showing student/senior discounts survive disclosure only because of ID gating that algorithmic signals cannot replicate. PRO's counter in [A4.4] — that a discount which dies on being named was never earned by need, only by ignorance — reframed the same mechanism as an indictment rather than a defense, and CON's closing never dissolved that fork.</best_rebuttal>
